entities.name: Psusennes II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Titkheperure or Tyetkheperre Psusennes II, known in Greek as Ψουσέννης and in Egyptian as Hor-Pasebakhaenniut II, presided over the final years of the Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt, reigning from approximately 959 BCE to 945 BCE. His rule from Tanis represented the twilight of a period characterized by fragmented authority, where the pharaohs in the Delta shared power—or merely nominal suzerainty—with the High Priests of Amun at Thebes. Psusennes II's significance lies not in grand achievements, but in his role as the transitional figure whose death marked the definitive end of the Tanite lineage and paved the way for a new era of Libyan dominance.

The historical record for Psusennes II's reign is notably sparse, underscoring the diminished central power of the pharaoh during this phase of the Third Intermediate Period. Unlike his more well-attested predecessors, evidence of major building projects, military campaigns, or extensive diplomatic engagements from his time is largely absent. His rule essentially maintained the delicate political equilibrium established by his predecessors, navigating the complex relationship with the powerful Theban priesthood, notably during the tenure of High Priest Pinedjem II. Archaeological finds, primarily from Tanis, offer limited insights, suggesting a continuation of existing religious and administrative practices rather than significant innovations.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Psusennes II, as the last pharaoh of the Twenty-first Dynasty, holds significant regional importance for marking the peaceful end of one dynastic line and directly ushering in the Libyan-led Twenty-second Dynasty, fundamentally altering Egyptian political leadership for two centuries.
